      1. The argument, in order
      Notation used on this pagesymbols, meanings, shapes
      01

      The image encoder now has language as a training partner.

      A caption can supply supervision

      The earlier parts built image representations from patches and from relationships between images. CLIP connects those representations to text. Its training example is an image together with the caption that accompanied it. The learning problem is to recognize those pairings among other images and captions in the batch.

      Radford and colleagues trained CLIP on 400 million internet image-text pairs and evaluated transfer without training a new classifier on each target dataset. We will use three tiny pairs to inspect the objective. The original CLIP paper describes the full models and experiments.

      "Two mugs on a table" and "a blue book in front of the mugs" both fit. Neither caption needs to describe everything.

      Relations and attributes matter, not just the object names.

      For exact arithmetic, switch to these three small grids. Their observed pairings are positives; the six crossed pairings are treated as negatives.

      The two encoders have different parameters but return vectors of the same width.

      Here the width is three. These are global embeddings $g^{\mathrm{img}}$ and $g^{\mathrm{txt}}$, not the attention value vectors $v_j$.

      What this toy replaces

      The image branch is a learned linear map of 16 pixels. The text branch sums learned rows for words in an eleven-word vocabulary. There is no pretrained visual or language knowledge, no image augmentation, and no attention inside these toy encoders. The matching objective, unit normalization, and gradient update are computed exactly. This lets us examine the part of CLIP that connects the two modalities without repeating the full ViT calculation.

      02

      Compute the vectors before comparing them.

      Pixels and words become comparable vectors

      Flatten the image in row-major order. Multiplying that sixteen-number row by $W_{\mathrm{img}}\in\mathbb R^{16\times3}$ produces one three-number image vector. For text, count the occurrences of each word and multiply by $W_{\mathrm{txt}}\in\mathbb R^{11\times3}$. The initial weights are chosen for readable arithmetic. Training can change every entry.

      $\ve{g_1^{\mathrm{img}}}=\underbrace{\operatorname{flatten}(I_1)}_{1\times16}\underbrace{W_{\mathrm{img}}}_{16\times3}=\ve{(2,1,0)}$

      These are the only nonzero starting rows. The anchor has $(1,0,0)$ at pixels 1, 3, and 7.

      pixels = images.flatten(start_dim=1)  # [3, 16]
g_img = pixels @ W_img                # [3, 3]

      $\vq{g_1^{\mathrm{txt}}}=(1,0,0)+(0,0,0)+(1,0,0)=\vq{(2,0,0)}$

      counts = word_counts(captions)  # [3, 11], toy vocabulary
g_txt = counts @ W_txt          # [3, 3]

      This toy ignores word order. Real CLIP's text Transformer uses sequence information.

      $\ve{\hat g_1^{\mathrm{img}}}=\dfrac{\ve{(2,1,0)}}{\sqrt{2^2+1^2}}\approx\ve{(0.894,0.447,0)}$

      $\vq{\hat g_1^{\mathrm{txt}}}=\dfrac{\vq{(2,0,0)}}{2}=\vq{(1,0,0)}$

      g_img_unit = F.normalize(g_img, dim=-1)
g_txt_unit = F.normalize(g_txt, dim=-1)

      Both lengths are now one. Their dot product measures cosine similarity rather than the size of either vector.

      Every row is unit length at full precision. Three-decimal displays may not have a norm of exactly one.

      The complete starting maps

      The encoders output a whole-image or whole-caption vector. A real model has many internal token embeddings and attention values before this global output. Shared output width does not imply that the two encoder architectures, internal widths, or parameters are the same.

      03

      One dot product becomes a matrix of candidate matches.

      Compare every image with every caption

      We have three image vectors and three text vectors. Compare every image with every caption, including captions from the other pairs. The cosine matrix $C$ is $3\times3$: its row chooses an image, and its column chooses a caption. It is a matrix of matches between whole examples, not an attention map between token positions.

      $\ve{\hat g_1^{\mathrm{img}}}=(2/\sqrt5,1/\sqrt5,0),\quad\vq{\hat g_1^{\mathrm{txt}}}=(1,0,0)$

      $C_{11}=(2/\sqrt5)\times1+(1/\sqrt5)\times0+0\times0$

      $C_{11}=2/\sqrt5\approx0.894$

      This is the two-square image matched against two bright squares. It is a similarity, not yet a probability.

      cosine = g_img_unit @ g_txt_unit.T  # [3, 3]
# rows: images; columns: captions

      Stripes also score $0.800$ against the dot caption: the encoders still confuse some pairs.

      $S=C/\tau,\qquad\tau=0.5\quad\Rightarrow\quad S=2C$

      logits = log_scale.exp() * cosine  # [3, 3]
# exp(log_scale) = 1 / temperature

      The denominator contains all three candidate captions for this one image.

      What changing temperature can and cannot do

      For fixed vectors and a fixed candidate set, a positive temperature changes the sharpness of softmax but not the highest-scoring candidate. The ratio of two candidate probabilities is $\exp((C_a-C_b)/\tau)$. A cosine gap of $0.05$ at $\tau=0.01$ therefore gives a ratio of $e^5\approx148.4$, not a five-fold ratio.

      The released CLIP implementation stores a learned logit_scale and exponentiates it. Its initialization is $\log(1/0.07)$; $0.07$ is the corresponding initial temperature. It is not a universal fixed temperature for every model or use case.

      04

      Each observed pair must be retrievable from either side.

      Train retrieval in both directions

      Image-to-text training asks each image to choose its observed caption. Text-to-image training asks each caption to choose its observed image. Both use the same logits, but they normalize over different candidates. Averaging the two losses trains both retrieval directions.

      The target indices are $[0,1,2]$: row 1 wants caption 1, row 2 wants caption 2, and row 3 wants caption 3.

      targets = torch.arange(3)
loss_image = F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)

      $\vd{L_{I\to T}}=-\frac13\sum_{i=1}^3\log\va{p(T_i\mid I_i,\mathcal B)}$

      Competitor captions affect the denominator even though the target is one diagonal entry.

      loss_text = F.cross_entropy(logits.T, targets)
# Each original column is now a candidate-image row.

      For one bright dot, stripes and the dot initially tie at cosine $0.800$.

      loss = 0.5 * (loss_image + loss_text)
# Both cross-entropies already average over the 3 examples.

      Different normalizers give different losses in the two directions.

      For a batch of $N$ pairs, the loss is $-\frac{1}{2N}\sum_i[\log p(T_i\mid I_i,\mathcal B)+\log p(I_i\mid T_i,\mathcal B)]$. Rows and columns are supervised separately; neither direction solves a global one-to-one assignment problem. During inference, two different images may legitimately retrieve the same description.

      05

      The similarity matrix is computed; the encoder parameters are learned.

      A wrong match changes both encoders

      Our first forward pass ends at a loss of about $0.578$. The computation graph connects that loss to the two parameter matrices and to the log scale. Backpropagation follows those connections through both softmax directions, every dot product, and the normalization of each vector. The optimizer then updates the parameters. The next forward pass recomputes the embeddings and the matching matrix.

      optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

      Update $W_{\mathrm{img}}$, $W_{\mathrm{txt}}$, and log scale. Recompute the vectors, scores, and probabilities.

      The learning rate is $0.1$. The displayed parameter is one of 82 learned numbers; the step updates all of them together.

      What was checked

      The numerical engine includes the exact derivative of $g/\lVert g\rVert_2$, averages both cross-entropies over the batch, and computes every gradient before changing any parameter. Central finite differences check all 82 parameter gradients. A separate NumPy implementation reproduces the forward pass, one-step update, and 60-step checkpoint.

      The next section freezes the checkpoint after 60 steps. Its mean loss on these three training pairs is . That small number describes this toy batch only. It is not an accuracy measurement on unseen data.

      06

      After training, choose descriptions without fitting a new class head.

      The candidate text supplies the classifier

      Keep both encoders fixed. For each candidate class, write a description and encode it into a unit text vector. Those text vectors are the classifier's weight rows: the image vector scores each candidate with a dot product. Changing the candidate list changes the readout without changing the learned encoders.

      For pretrained CLIP, this is zero-shot classification when no training on labeled examples from the target task is used. Our tiny checkpoint has already seen the three displayed images and descriptions, so its scores illustrate the inference mechanism rather than demonstrating zero-shot transfer.

      The candidate list defines the comparison. No model scores are shown here.

      Each description becomes a candidate vector. No optimizer step happens here.

      g_txt_unit = F.normalize(text_encoder(prompts), dim=-1)
scores = g_img_unit @ g_txt_unit.T
choice = scores.argmax(dim=-1)

      Same two-square image. Same three descriptions. Encoder checkpoint: 60 training steps.

      Softmax normalizes over these supplied descriptions. It does not enumerate every possible object or sentence.

      The toy uses only its eleven listed words, not a pretrained language model.

      scores = g_txt_unit @ cached_image_vectors.T
ranked_images = scores.argsort(descending=True)

      Image-to-text retrieval uses the same operation with the roles reversed.

      Prompts are part of the evaluation

      A class name can be ambiguous: crane may mean a bird or a machine. A description can specify the intended sense. The CLIP paper evaluates prompt templates such as a photo of a {label} and averages normalized text embeddings across templates, then normalizes the result. Prompt choice can help, but no wording guarantees an improvement on every dataset. See the paper's prompt experiments.

      The current toy template adds word rows according to its bag-of-words rule. Template-only words such as grid retain their hand-chosen starting rows because the training captions do not contain them. The toy cannot show the full contextual behavior of a text Transformer. In a real deployment, report the candidate set and prompt policy alongside accuracy, and evaluate on held-out task data.

      07

      Keep the scope of the objective and the candidate set visible.

      A match score is not a truth judgment

      There are two different claims to separate. Contrastive training can learn representations that transfer to new tasks. A particular softmax score, however, only compares the candidates supplied to it. Removing the correct candidate does not create an automatic "none of the above" output. Evaluation must account for that limitation.

      $\va{p(T_j\mid I,\mathcal C)}=\dfrac{\exp(C_j/\tau)}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal C}\exp(C_k/\tau)}$

      • The candidate set $\mathcal C$ is chosen by us.
      • Adding or removing a candidate changes the denominator.
      • A smaller temperature can make the winner look more certain without adding image evidence.

      A high candidate probability is not calibrated confidence that a description is true in the world.

      Keep the two-square image. Offer only one bright dot.

      One score $s$ gives $\va{p}=\dfrac{e^s}{e^s}$.

      Two images may share a valid description. A one-positive-per-row batch objective still treats the other pairing as a negative.

      Batch construction, duplicate handling, and richer positive sets matter. Larger batches can add both useful competitors and false negatives.

      image + candidate descriptions → scores → retrieve or classify

      image + a language decoder → next-token probabilities → generated answer

      CLIP provides a visual-language matching representation. The next part adds a language model that can produce words.

      Zero-shot means no task-specific training in that evaluation. The encoders have already learned from image-text data.

      Try a real model separately

      The original browser CLIP demo accepts photos and candidate prompts and downloads a pretrained model. It requires network access and browser support; nothing in this lesson depends on it. Its pretrained embeddings must not be confused with the three-coordinate toy used here. The official CLIP examples show normalization, zero-shot classification, and caching text features.

      Checks before using this in an application

      Evaluate the specific images, language, candidate classes, and errors that matter for the task. Pretraining on web captions does not remove biases or guarantee robust counting, spatial reasoning, or domain transfer. The CLIP model card records intended uses and limitations.

      Why a collapsed representation is not useful

      If every image and every caption returns the same unit vector, all scores tie. Each candidate then receives $1/N$, so each directional loss is $\log N$. With three pairs, that is . The objective rewards identifying the observed partner among competitors, not simply increasing every match score together.

      The complete toy parameters and a reproducible training script are stored with this article. All displayed calculations retain full precision internally; rounding happens only when a number is rendered.
